source.title: Compatibility of Face Embeddings Across Deep Neural Networks
source.authors: Fizza Rubab; Yi-Ying Tong; Arun Ross

record.tranche_reason: The study tests whether independently trained models' face embeddings can be aligned, using affine mappings and face-identification/verification outcomes rather than a direct sweep of representation similarity with scale.
record.gate_note: The reported results concern alignment of face embeddings across models and datasets. Results cited from prior work are not recorded as rows. Tables 2 and 3 contain many separate model-pair, method, dataset and metric results; only a subset is retained under the 60-row limit. No scale sweep is reported.
record.test_reason: The study directly tests cross-model representational compatibility using supervised affine maps and held-out face identification and verification. It also tests dataset dependence and documents incomplete compatibility; it does not test increasing convergence with scale.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is substantially accurate. The authors interpret strong affine-map transfer as evidence that independently trained models share facial-identity geometry, report stable model families and directional asymmetry, and question inherent template revocability. Their common-manifold explanation is an interpretation; the experiments do not establish its causal origin or convergence with scale.
record.recipe_differences: The study fits supervised affine mappings between final face embeddings and evaluates identification/verification transfer; it does not reproduce a seed-based shared-feature or representation-similarity procedure. It tests linear, orthogonal Procrustes and Ridge alignment.
record.method_sensitivity: Results vary by model family and pair, dataset, direction of mapping, and task. Cross-dataset foundation-model identification declines relative to intra-dataset results; the study also reports lower foundation-model verification than face-specific verification.
record.peer_reviewed: Accepted at IEEE/IAPR International Joint Conference on Biometrics (IJCB), September 2026
record.problems: No scale or capability sweep, so the study does not establish convergence increasing with model size or performance. The alignment experiments use shared face images and identity-disjoint training/test splits; they do not establish why compatibility arises. Foundation-model verification and some model-pair/dataset outcomes remain substantially weaker than face-specific results. Many table results are omitted here due to the row limit.
record.rows_left_out: Tables 2 and 3 report separate values for additional model-pair × method × dataset × metric combinations. These are not individually extracted beyond the selected aggregate results and SAM → InternVL3 examples, to stay within the 60-row limit; the omitted results are in Tables 2 and 3.

untested.parts: No model-size or capability sweep tests whether alignment increases as models improve.
No paired image-caption comparison between vision and language representations; multimodal model names do not establish cross-modal convergence.
No independently trained initialization-seed comparison. The five experimental seeds change evaluation partitions or sampling.
No stitching, relative representations, unpaired alignment, or broad representation-domain test. Missing native within-model controls prevent directly establishing little performance loss.
No recurring interpretable features, neurons, SAE features, or circuits are identified.
No systematic similarity-metric or neighbourhood-setting sweep. Identification, AUC and TMR are downstream performance measures rather than interchangeable representation-similarity metrics.
No scale plateau or causal intervention on shared training data or objectives. Recognition accuracy does not quantify the fraction of shared representational geometry.

missing.what: Training-data sensitivity: Procrustes and Ridge exceed 70% identification accuracy with 10% training data, whereas unconstrained linear alignment initially overfits and improves with more data. The figure's pair label is difficult to read in the supplied text.
Directional asymmetry: mean Rank-1 difference of 15.7 percentage points, with extremes exceeding 49; target-space quality and dimensionality affect compatibility.
Foundation-model TMR falls below 15% for most pairs at FMR=0.1%; this is a separate security-threshold result currently confined to a note.

The authors report improved embedding-level RSA and CKA after linear mapping, and little additional gain from quadratic or MLP maps. The referenced supplementary results and numerical values are absent from the supplied text.
Stable model-family clustering across datasets, including separation of SAM and grouping by training objective; this is descriptive evidence, not a causal test of training objectives.

record.verdict_notes: This is not an original source for any version. The supplied text contains unclear aggregate weighting and apparent summary/table inconsistencies, so aggregate numbers remain explicitly author-reported. High cross-model task accuracy supports operational interchangeability, while absent native within-model controls limit conclusions about little loss or geometric completeness. Additional Table 2 and Table 3 entries were declared omitted and are not counted as missing.

versions.untested_parts: No model size or capability sweep; no test of whether alignment rises with scale or performance.
No direct comparison of vision and language representations for paired images and captions, or of alignment as both models improve.
No comparison of different initialization seeds of the same architecture or analysis of shared features/subspaces.

Tests supervised affine/linear alignment using paired face-image embeddings. Does not test stitching, relative representations, unpaired alignment, or whether mappings work with little loss for arbitrary representations.
No recurring interpretable neurons, SAE features, or circuits are examined.

Tests transfer between face datasets and reports differences between identification and verification outcomes. Does not vary nearest-neighbour count or systematically compare representation-similarity measures/settings.

Shows incomplete alignment for some model families and performance decline across datasets. Does not test a plateau with scale or establish whether shared data/objectives, rather than a common model of reality, cause alignment.
